name: Ulmus

project_scope.selection_mode: five-species photo-led Central Texas elm comparison
project_scope.note: Five installed learner species: four native project elms plus introduced Chinese elm as a high-value comparison. Winged elm was added after its completed range review; preserve Chinese elm as FAIL/introduced comparison.

priority: corky twig wings and whether they stop at nodes
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify elms from leaf shape alone. Cedar vs winged elm especially depends on wing behavior at nodes and reproductive season.

quick_key.if: regular corky wings on branches, wings usually stop abruptly at nodes, pointed small leaves, SPRING flowers/fruit
small rough leaves + FALL flowers/fruit + corky ridges/wings may continue around nodes
large strongly asymmetric leaf + normally unwinged twig + SPRING samara with ciliate margin
large thick sandpaper leaf + reddish hairy/tomentose buds + samara hairy on the body
mottled exfoliating lacebark + small glossy smoother leaves + FALL reproduction
quick_key.then: Ulmus parvifolia — Chinese elm, introduced comparison

look_here_first: FIRST inspect the TWIG for corky wings. SECOND feel/inspect a COMPLETE LEAF for size, roughness, asymmetrical base, and venation. THIRD use the CALENDAR: winged/American/slippery elm reproduce in spring, while cedar elm and Chinese elm reproduce late summer-fall. FOURTH inspect the SAMARA and bark. Do not identify an elm from leaf shape alone.
shared_traits: Alternate simple leaves with pinnate side veins and usually an asymmetrical leaf base.
Small wind-pollinated flowers; most project native elms flower before or near leaf-out, but cedar elm is a major fall-flowering exception.
Dry winged samaras are the key Ulmus fruit; margin hair, body hair, notch shape and season help separate species.
Corky twig wings occur in both winged elm and cedar elm, so the presence of wings alone is not enough.

genus_diagnostics.twig_wings: U. alata and U. crassifolia can both be corky-winged. In winged elm, regular wings commonly terminate abruptly at nodes; cedar-elm wings/ridges can be more intermittent or continue around nodes.
genus_diagnostics.leaf: American and slippery elm have much larger strongly asymmetric leaves. Slippery elm is especially thick and sandpaper-rough with reddish hairy buds. Cedar elm has small rough leaves; Chinese elm has small smoother glossy leaves.
genus_diagnostics.season: Spring reproduction strongly favors U. alata, U. americana, or U. rubra. Late-summer/fall flowers and samaras strongly favor U. crassifolia or introduced U. parvifolia.
genus_diagnostics.samara: American elm has a ciliate samara margin; slippery elm is hairy on the samara body; cedar elm samaras are small and pubescent; winged elm has small spring samaras with hairy/ciliate margins; Chinese elm has a small glabrous fall samara.
genus_diagnostics.bark: Chinese elm's exfoliating mottled lacebark is a strong tie-breaker. Native project elms lack that distinctive patchwork exfoliation.

comparison_cards.title: Winged elm vs cedar elm
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both can have corky wings. Follow a wing to the NODE and then check the reproductive season.
comparison_cards.rule: U. alata: regular wings commonly stop at nodes + spring flowers/samaras. U. crassifolia: small rough leaves + late-summer/fall reproduction; corky ridges may continue around nodes.
comparison_cards.warning: Do not call a tree winged elm solely because a twig is corky-winged.

comparison_cards.title: American elm vs slippery elm
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both have large asymmetric leaves. Feel the upper surface, inspect buds, then check samara hair placement.
comparison_cards.rule: U. rubra is markedly sandpaper-rough with reddish hairy buds and a hairy samara body; U. americana has a ciliate samara margin and less diagnostic red-tomentose buds.

comparison_cards.title: Small native elms vs Chinese elm
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Check bark, leaf texture, twig wings and season together.
comparison_cards.rule: Chinese elm: mottled exfoliating lacebark + glossy smoother leaves + fall fruit. Cedar/winged elm: native rougher leaves and/or corky wings, with cedar fall-fruiting and winged spring-fruiting.

visual_comparison.title: Five elms: twig wings, leaf texture, season and samaras
visual_comparison.subtitle: Five matched canonical elm species now have physically installed photographs (six JPEG/PNG total). Specialty same-scale twig nodes, hairy buds, and full samara comparisons still pending.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: WINGS? follow them to the NODE. BIG LEAF? compare American vs slippery. FALL FRUIT? think cedar or Chinese. SPRING FRUIT + corky wings? winged elm.

part_examples.title: Verified winged elm foliage; corky-wing example remains disputed
part_examples.look_for: Pointed, serrated winged-elm leaves in the installed exact-species image. Twig wing/node placement is NOT shown by this photo; don't teach the disputed former twig as diagnostic proof.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A verified foliage example for winged elm. Branch/node characters require a different, independently identified photo.

part_examples.title: Read cedar elm leaves and samaras
part_examples.look_for: Small rough leaves and winged samaras; pair with a fall-season observation and twig-wing view.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Cedar elm is the common Central Texas anchor and the main winged-elm look-alike.

part_examples.title: Use American elm's large asymmetric leaf
part_examples.look_for: Large double-serrate leaves with a strongly uneven base beside flat spring samaras.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Separates the large-leaved native elm group from cedar and winged elm.

part_examples.title: Feel the slippery-elm clue
part_examples.look_for: A thick strongly asymmetric leaf with a very rough upper surface; then verify reddish hairy buds.
part_examples.why_it_matters: American and slippery elm overlap in leaf size, so texture and buds become the tie-breakers.

part_examples.title: Spot Chinese elm's lacebark
part_examples.look_for: Patchy exfoliating tan/orange/gray bark paired with small glossy leaves.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Keeps the common planted/naturalized non-native from being mistaken for a native small-leaf elm.
